title: The surprising decline in violence | Steven Pinker
summary: Steven Pinker's 2007 TED talk argues violence, including war between states, has declined over millennia, centuries and decades, and offers four explanations.

assertions.quote: were far more violent than we are, that violence has been in decline
had prevailed during the 20th century, there would have been two billion deaths

verdicts.note: Ethnographic and archaeological data show high rates of violent death, though the samples are selective and the size of the gap is disputed.

assertions.quote: decline in interstate wars, in deadly ethnic riots or pogroms and in military coups,
two orders of magnitude in homicide from the Middle Ages to the present

verdicts.note: Eisner's compilation of European records shows homicide falling from tens per 100,000 to about one.

assertions.quote: living in the most peaceful time in our species's existence.

verdicts.note: Per-capita violent death is low by historical standards, but battle deaths rose sharply in the 2020s with Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan.

PRIO: 2021-2025 was the most violent period since the Cold War ended, with over 930,000 killed, about as many as in the 20 years before, so the present is not the most peaceful time even in recent decades.
UCDP: 244,600 killed in organized violence in 2025, the second-highest total since 1994, with the number of state-based conflicts doubling since 2010; the most peaceful recent years were before 2014.
OWID: fewer people died in conflicts in recent decades than in most of the 20th century, but recent rises in the Middle East, Africa and Europe make the trend uncertain.

assertions.quote: become more valuable alive than dead, and violence declines for selfish reasons.

verdicts.note: Commercial-peace studies find a modest effect, but dense trade did not prevent 1914 or Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

assertions.quote: of the decline of homicide in Europe coincided with the rise

verdicts.note: Homicide fell as states consolidated and violence clusters in failed states, but correlation in timing is not proof of the mechanism.

assertions.quote: There's a cognitive illusion. We cognitive psychologists know that the easier it is to recall

verdicts.note: The availability bias is well established, but how much of public belief about violence it explains is less measured.
